$comment: Cross-runtime golden vectors for Ion's three float widths (f2/f4/f8).
Consumed by all three in-repo runtimes; the three implementations must produce
byte-identical CBOR for the same value.

rule.declaredWidth: Every float is written at its DECLARED width: f2 -> 0xF9 + 2 bytes, f4 -> 0xFA + 4 bytes, f8 -> 0xFB + 8 bytes, always, regardless of value.
rule.why: Ion is schema-first — the field's width is declared in the contract, so the wire honours it. Shortest-form encoding would make f2 and f4 indistinguishable in a capture, would require reimplementing identical shrink logic in three runtimes, and would make golden vectors runtime-dependent (breaking any future signing, hashing, dedup or content-addressing of payloads).
rule.readAcceptsEveryWidth: Readers MUST accept f9, fa and fb for EVERY float type, in both directions: an f4 field may receive an f8-encoded value and an f8 field may receive an f2-encoded one. Widening from a narrower wire width is exact; narrowing from a wider one rounds. This is what makes the rule non-wire-breaking — payloads written by a peer that shrank floats still decode. See the `crossWidth` vectors.
rule.history: System.Formats.Cbor's CborWriter.WriteSingle/WriteDouble shrink a float to the shortest lossless CBOR float in every conformance mode except Ctap2Canonical (1.5f -> 'f93e00', 4f -> 'f94400', and a double could shrink all the way to float16), while packages/ion.webcore.js and packages/ion.rustcore (minicbor) always emitted the declared width. C# now forces the width via CborWriter.WriteEncodedValue with a hand-built header + big-endian payload, which works in all four conformance modes and leaves the writer's mode alone — switching to Ctap2Canonical would also mandate sorted map keys and forbid indefinite lengths, breaking Partial<T>'s declaration-order map (see partial.golden.json).

canonicalNaN.rule: NaN is canonicalised on write to the positive quiet NaN with an empty payload.
canonicalNaN.why: This is required for byte identity, not cosmetic. .NET's float.NaN has the sign bit SET (ffc00000) while Rust's f32::NAN and JavaScript's NaN literal are positive (7fc00000) — and a JS engine does not even guarantee that: Math.sqrt(-1) yields a sign-set NaN that survives a Float32Array store as ffc00000. JavaScript cannot observe or reproduce a NaN payload at all, so canonicalising is the only agreement the three runtimes can reach. Writers therefore emit these bits for ANY NaN input, including signalling NaNs and NaNs with a payload.
canonicalNaN.notCanonicalised: Every other special value is written bit-for-bit. In particular -0.0 is preserved as -0.0 (f2 8000 / f4 80000000 / f8 8000000000000000) and is NOT folded into +0.0.

howToConsume: encode: build the value from `bits` (IEEE-754 bit pattern, big-endian hex, `payloadBytes` wide),
write it with the runtime's formatter for `type`, expect exactly `hex`.
decode: read `hex` with the runtime's formatter for `type`, re-encode it, expect `hex` back.
For each entry of `crossWidth`: read `hex` with the formatter for `type` (note the wire width
differs from the declared width), re-encode, expect `reencodedHex`.

vectors.name: f2-1.1
vectors.notes: Nearest f2 to 1.1. The value 1.1 was the one the old partial vectors used to sidestep the shrinking bug.

vectors.name: f2-nan
vectors.notes: Canonical positive quiet NaN. Writers must emit this for ANY NaN input.

vectors.name: f4-zero
vectors.notes: REGRESSION GUARD. The old C# writer shrank this to 'f90000'.

vectors.name: f4-1.5
vectors.notes: REGRESSION GUARD. The old C# writer shrank this to 'f93e00'.

vectors.name: f4-4
vectors.notes: REGRESSION GUARD. The old C# writer shrank this to 'f94400'.

vectors.name: f4-1.1
vectors.notes: Not representable in f2, so this was the ONE value all three runtimes already agreed on — which is why the partial vectors used it.

vectors.name: f4-min-subnormal
vectors.notes: Smallest positive subnormal f4. Does not fit f2, so it never shrank.

vectors.name: f4-nan
vectors.notes: Canonical positive quiet NaN. .NET's float.NaN is ffc00000 and JS's Math.sqrt(-1) is ffc00000; both must still write fa7fc00000. Old C#: 'f97e00'.

vectors.name: f8-zero
vectors.notes: REGRESSION GUARD. The old C# writer shrank a double all the way to f2: 'f90000'.

vectors.name: f8-nan
vectors.notes: Canonical positive quiet NaN. .NET's double.NaN is fff8000000000000 and must still write fb7ff8000000000000. Old C#: 'f97e00'.

crossWidth.name: f2-reads-f4
crossWidth.notes: An f2 field receiving an f4-encoded 1.5. minicbor's Decoder::f16 and .NET's CborReader.ReadHalf both reject this natively; both runtimes dispatch on the wire width instead.

crossWidth.name: f2-reads-f8
crossWidth.notes: An f2 field receiving an f8-encoded 1.5.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-f2
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. This is exactly what the previous C# release wrote for 1.5f. New readers must still accept it, so old payloads keep decoding.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-f8
crossWidth.notes: An f4 field receiving an f8-encoded 1.5. minicbor's Decoder::f32 and .NET's CborReader.ReadSingle both reject fb natively.

crossWidth.name: f8-reads-f2
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. What the previous C# release wrote for 1.5d.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-zero
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Previous C# release's encoding of 0f.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-neg-zero
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. -0.0 survives the legacy round-trip as -0.0.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-4
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Previous C# release's encoding of 4f.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-nan
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Previous C# release's encoding of float.NaN.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-pos-inf
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Previous C# release's encoding of +Inf.

crossWidth.name: f4-reads-legacy-neg-inf
crossWidth.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Previous C# release's encoding of -Inf.
